title: The arch behind the scaffolding
allegory: A progress measure is like an engineer's gauge on an arch being built behind scaffolding: the traffic count looks unchanged for months, but a gauge designed from the blueprint shows the arch taking more load every week, long before the scaffolding comes down.
map: the traffic count over the bridge
test loss: flat for thousands of epochs, then a sudden drop
scaffolding that carries only the trucks it was built for
memorisation: train loss near zero, no generalisation
the arch, built stone by stone behind it
the Fourier circuit: key frequencies combined by angle addition
a gauge designed from the blueprint
a progress measure derived from the hypothesised circuit
pull one set of arch stones and see how much worse it carries
excluded loss: delete one key frequency's cos(w(x+y)) and sin(w(x+y)) parts, recompute training loss

props.label: test loss: flat for thousands of epochs

cap.1: A small model learns clock-style addition. It memorises its examples fast, then looks stuck for thousands of rounds. Suddenly it gets new ones right.
cap.2: Grokking: on addition mod 113, train loss hits zero quickly while test loss sits flat for thousands of epochs, then falls off a cliff. Was the model really idle all that time?
cap.3: The loss curve suggests a discontinuity: memorisation, a long plateau, abrupt generalisation. The question is whether the weights change during the plateau in ways the loss can't see.

cap.1: A bridge crew: scaffolding carries today's trucks while an arch rises behind it, stone by stone. From the road nothing changes until the scaffolding goes.
cap.2: Memorisation is the scaffolding: it handles the training set only. The general algorithm is the arch, built gradually underneath. The visible jump is mostly the scaffolding being removed.
cap.3: Three phases: memorisation, circuit formation, cleanup. Test loss moves mostly in cleanup, when memorising components are removed; the generalising circuit was being amplified throughout.

parts.note: one key frequency's cos and sin, deleted

cap.1: With the blueprint, build a gauge: pull one set of arch stones and measure how much worse the bridge carries. If it relies on the arch, that hurts.
cap.2: Excluded loss: take the training logits, delete the cos(w(x+y)) and sin(w(x+y)) components for one key frequency, and recompute the loss. It rises as the model comes to rely on that frequency.
cap.3: Deleting an equal-norm random direction costs far less: the signature of a mechanism being amplified. Its twin, restricted loss, keeps only the trig-sum directions and comes out lower than the full loss.

cap.1: Plot the gauge beside the traffic count. Test loss sits flat, then drops. The gauge climbs thousands of rounds earlier: the arch was taking load all along.
cap.2: Illustrative curves. Excluded loss rises well before the grokking point, while test loss is still flat. The mechanism was forming the whole time; the loss just couldn't show it.
cap.3: Excluded loss rises during the plateau and the visible test-loss drop coincides with cleanup, resolving grokking into memorisation, circuit formation and cleanup rather than a discontinuous emergence.

chapters.name: Off by one

left.title: raw argmax index
lines: deletes waves the model never used

chapters.verdict: A gauge built at the wrong frequency measures nothing. Check it against the logits.

cap.1: A classic slip: the frequency list starts at 1, not 0. Read it raw and every frequency is one too low, so your gauge watches stones the arch never used.
cap.2: The 2D Fourier helper's slice 0 holds frequency k = 1. Argmax without adding one and you get 13, 30, 34... Restricted and excluded loss are then computed at the wrong frequencies, quietly.
cap.3: Add one, then verify: reconstruct cos(w_k(x+y)) at each claimed key frequency and project the logits onto it. A wrong frequency projects to near nothing, which catches the off-by-one at once.

cap.1: So was it sudden? The loss says yes; the gauge says it grew steadily. Whether every 'sudden' skill in big AIs works this way is still argued.
cap.2: Current view: many abilities look like they switch on abruptly. Emerging: grokking's jump is continuous underneath, in a metric built from the mechanism. What you need: before calling a jump sudden, ask what that metric shows.
cap.3: The argument: emergent capabilities may be discontinuous only in the metric you watch, not underneath. Grokking supports it with a known mechanism; for large models, whose mechanisms are mostly unknown, it stays an argument.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Measure the mechanism, not just the loss
See a skill forming before it shows
Same move in evals and phase-transition work

cap.1: Understand the mechanism and you can watch it grow before any score moves. That early view is what understanding and steering AI training needs.
cap.2: Progress measures turn a mechanism into a metric that moves before the loss does. The same move carries into evals and into phase-transition work generally.
cap.3: Deriving the metric from the hypothesised mechanism both validates the mechanism (the metric should move) and exposes hidden training dynamics: a tool for understanding, and eventually steering, what models learn.

coda.title: Grow the arch, then take the scaffolding down

readouts.label: gauge: score lost at 50 when frequency 14 is deleted

caption.1: The horizontal axis is candidate answers; 50 is right. Grow the circuit and the gauge climbs while 50 stays buried in clutter. Then clean up: suddenly it wins.
caption.2: Circuit strength stands for training progress; deleting frequency 14 is the excluded-loss gauge. It rises with the circuit while the prediction is still wrong, and the win arrives with cleanup.
caption.3: Toy scores: a·Σ_k cos(w_k(50 − z)) plus clutter, keys 14, 31, 35, 41, 42, 52 (w_k = 2πk/113). Waves align at z = 50 and cancel elsewhere; the gauge tracks a, the visible win tracks cleanup.

where_else: Restricted loss: the same idea reversed, keep only the mechanism and watch performance hold
Phase-transition work: tracking a behaviour forming during training with a mechanism-derived metric
Evals: measuring a capability's ingredients, not just pass or fail
Engineering monitoring: gauges designed from the blueprint, not read off the output

hamming.what: A metric derived from a hypothesised circuit, such as excluded loss, that tracks the mechanism forming even while the loss is flat.
hamming.when: When training looks stalled or a capability seems to appear suddenly, and you have, or suspect, a mechanism behind it.
hamming.why: The loss shows only the final effect; a mechanism-derived metric shows progress early and tests the hypothesis at the same time.

object.title: The grokking landscape
object.subtitle: The model's scores for candidate answers around the right one, stretched out along training time: a ridge rising under clutter that melts away late.

cap.1: A landscape of the model's scores. Across: candidate answers around the right one, 50. Front to back: training time.
cap.2: Height is the logit for each candidate answer z (x-axis) at each point in training (y-axis), for the input pair whose sum is 50.
cap.3: Toy logit surface: a(t)·Σ_k cos(w_k(50 − z)) plus memorisation clutter that decays late, a two-phase stand-in for circuit formation and cleanup.

cap.1: Early on, the scores are bumpy clutter from memorisation. The right answer doesn't stand out yet.
cap.2: Early checkpoints: memorised components dominate, so the correct logit is buried and test loss is high.
cap.3: Memorisation phase: the generalising components are small relative to memorising ones, so on held-out inputs the argmax is wrong.

cap.1: Along training time, the ridge at the right answer rises steadily, long before the clutter clears. That rise is what a progress measure sees.
cap.2: The circuit's contribution grows through the plateau. A metric built from it moves while test loss doesn't.
cap.3: Circuit formation: the trig-sum component is amplified continuously; excluded loss, which removes it, therefore rises before grokking.

cap.1: Delete frequency 14 and the ridge sinks a little. The later in training, the more it sinks: that's excluded loss rising.
cap.2: Removing one key frequency lowers the correct logit by that frequency's share, which grows as the circuit strengthens.
cap.3: Excluded loss measures reliance on a frequency: its cost grows with that component's amplitude, and far exceeds the cost of an equal-norm random direction.

cap.1: At the end the clutter is gone and only the ridge remains. The jump everyone saw was mostly the cleanup.
cap.2: Late checkpoints: memorising components are removed, and the correct answer wins on new inputs.
cap.3: Cleanup phase: memorising components are removed, and the test-loss drop tracks this rather than the circuit's earlier formation.

predict.q: Test loss is flat, but excluded loss is climbing. What's happening?

options.t: The generalising circuit is forming underneath

predict.why: Excluded loss rises as the model comes to rely on the key frequencies, before the test loss can show it.

predict.q: Instead of a key frequency, you delete a random direction of the same size. Compared with excluded loss, the cost is...
predict.why: Excluded loss rises far more than an equal-norm random direction would cost: the signature of a real mechanism.

predict.q: Your key frequencies are all exactly one lower than the reference. What went wrong?

options.t: The Fourier helper indexes from k = 1; add one to the argmax

predict.why: Slice 0 holds frequency 1. Check by projecting the logits onto cos(w_k(x+y)): wrong frequencies project to near nothing.

object.where: Anywhere a hidden quantity grows before the visible one moves: capability evals, training phase transitions, a kettle's temperature before it boils.
